subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Public Goods Game
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Public Goods Game usable.

hook.text: Ten strangers each get $10. They can contribute to a shared pot that doubles and splits equally. Free riders ruin it.

buildup.text: In repeated rounds, contributions start high and decline. People cooperate at first, then punish free riders.

discovery.text: Adding a punishment option revives cooperation. People pay to punish free riders even at personal cost.

twist.text: Altruistic punishment is costly to the punisher. But it sustains the group norm. Without it, cooperation collapses.

climax.text: Real institutions mirror this. Taxes, fines, and social shame are formalized punishment that sustains cooperation.

punchline.text: Cooperation survives only when free riding has a cost.

quiz.question: What happens in public goods games when punishment is introduced?
options: Free riding increases because people resent the punishment
Cooperation revives as free riders are penalized

details.summary: In the public goods game, participants choose how much to contribute to a shared pool that is multiplied and divided equally. Self-interest says contribute nothing, but most people contribute substantially, and contribution levels depend heavily on perceived cooperation by others.
details.whyItMatters: The public goods game is the laboratory model of real-world collective action problems like taxation, team effort, and environmental protection. It reveals that people are neither purely selfish nor purely altruistic but conditionally cooperative.
takeaways: Initial contributions are typically 40 to 60 percent of endowments
Contributions decline over rounds as conditional cooperators see free-riding
Allowing punishment of free-riders sustains high cooperation levels

faq.question: What does the public goods game teach about real-world cooperation?
faq.answer: It shows cooperation is natural but fragile. People start willing to cooperate but reduce contributions when they perceive others free-riding. Sustaining cooperation requires either visible punishment of defectors or credible information that others are contributing.

faq.question: Does punishment improve cooperation in public goods games?
faq.answer: Dramatically. When players can pay to reduce free-riders' earnings, average contributions rise to near 100 percent. The threat of punishment deters free-riding, and most people willingly pay the cost to punish cheaters.
